verses.text: Solomon also built his own palace. It took him thirteen years to finish it all.

He built the Palace of the Forest of Lebanon. It was one hundred cubits long, fifty cubits wide, and thirty cubits high. It stood on four rows of cedar pillars, with cedar beams resting on the pillars.
The roof was made of cedar laid over the forty-five beams that rested on the pillars, fifteen beams in each row.
There were window frames in three rows, with windows facing each other in sets of three.
All the doorways and door posts had square frames, and the windows faced each other in sets of three.
He also made the Hall of Pillars. It was fifty cubits long and thirty cubits wide. In front of it was a porch with pillars and a roof over it.
He built the Hall of the Throne, also called the Hall of Justice, where he would judge the people. It was covered with cedar from floor to ceiling.

The palace where Solomon himself would live was built in another courtyard behind the hall, and it was made in the same way. He also built a palace like this hall for Pharaoh's daughter, whom he had married.

All these buildings were made from expensive stones, cut to size and smoothed with saws on the inside and outside. This was done from the foundation all the way to the top, and from the outside all the way to the great courtyard.
The foundations were laid with large, expensive stones, some ten cubits long and some eight cubits long.
Above them were more expensive stones, cut to size, and cedar beams.
The great courtyard was surrounded by a wall made of three rows of cut stone and one row of cedar beams, just like the inner courtyard of the LORD's temple and its porch.
King Solomon sent for Hiram and brought him from Tyre.

Hiram's mother was a widow from the tribe of Naphtali, and his father was a man from Tyre who worked with bronze. Hiram was full of wisdom, understanding, and skill to do every kind of bronze work. He came to King Solomon and did all the work he was given.
He made two bronze pillars. Each was eighteen cubits high and twelve cubits around.
He also made two tops of melted bronze to put on top of the pillars. Each top was five cubits high.
Each top had a net of criss-cross patterns and chains twisted together. There were seven on each top.
He made two rows of bronze pomegranates around each net to decorate the tops of the pillars. He did the same for both tops.
The tops of the pillars in the porch were shaped like lilies, four cubits high.
On the tops of both pillars, above the rounded part next to the net, there were two hundred pomegranates in rows all around.
He set up the pillars at the porch of the temple. The pillar on the south side he named Jakin, and the pillar on the north side he named Boaz.
The tops of the pillars were shaped like lilies. And so the work on the pillars was finished.
He made a large round bowl of melted bronze, called the Sea. It was ten cubits across from rim to rim and five cubits high. It was thirty cubits around.
Below its rim, all the way around, were two rows of gourds, ten to every cubit. They were cast in one piece with the Sea.
The Sea stood on twelve bronze bulls. Three faced north, three faced west, three faced south, and three faced east. The Sea rested on top of them, and their back ends faced the centre.
It was as thick as the width of a hand. Its rim was like the rim of a cup, shaped like a lily flower. It held two thousand baths of water, about forty-four thousand litres.
He also made ten bronze stands. Each was four cubits long, four cubits wide, and three cubits high.
This is how the stands were made: they had side panels attached to frames.
On the panels between the frames were lions, bulls, and winged creatures. On the frames above and below the lions and bulls were hanging decorations shaped like wreaths.
Each stand had four bronze wheels with bronze axles. At the four corners were supports for a basin, cast with wreaths on each side.
Inside the stand was a round opening one cubit deep, with a frame around it one and a half cubits across. Around the opening there were carvings. The side panels of the stands were square, not round.
The four wheels were under the panels, and the axles of the wheels were joined to the stand. Each wheel was one and a half cubits high.
The wheels were made like chariot wheels. Their axles, rims, spokes, and hubs were all made of cast metal.
Each stand had four handles, one at each corner, made in one piece with the stand.
At the top of each stand was a round band half a cubit high. The supports and panels at the top were made in one piece with the stand.
He carved winged creatures, lions, and palm trees on the surfaces of the supports and panels, wherever there was space, with wreaths all around.
This is how he made the ten stands. They were all cast in the same mould and were the same size and shape.
Then he made ten bronze basins. Each basin held forty baths of water and measured four cubits across. There was one basin for each of the ten stands.
He put five stands on the south side of the temple and five on the north side. He put the Sea on the south side, at the south-east corner of the temple.
Hiram also made pots, shovels, and bowls. So Hiram finished all the work King Solomon had given him to do for the LORD's temple:
the two pillars, the two bowl-shaped tops on the pillars, and the two nets that covered the two bowl-shaped tops on the pillars;
the four hundred pomegranates for the two nets, two rows of pomegranates for each net, covering the bowl-shaped tops on the pillars;
the ten stands and the ten basins on the stands;
the Sea and the twelve bulls under it;
and the pots, shovels, and bowls. All these things that Hiram made for King Solomon for the LORD's temple were made of polished bronze.
The king had them cast in clay moulds in the plain of the Jordan, between Sukkoth and Zarethan.
Solomon did not weigh any of these things, because there were so many. The weight of the bronze was never known.
Solomon also made all the things that were in the LORD's temple: the gold altar, and the gold table where the special bread was placed before God;
the lampstands of pure gold, five on the south side and five on the north, in front of the inner room; and the gold flowers, lamps, and tongs;
the pure gold cups, wick trimmers, bowls, dishes, and fire pans; and the gold hinges for the doors of the inner room, the Most Holy Place, and for the doors of the main hall of the temple.

So all the work King Solomon did for the LORD's temple was finished. Then he brought in the things his father David had set apart for God, the silver, the gold, and the other objects, and put them in the treasure rooms of the LORD's temple.
